newsitem.title: COTE D'IVOIRE: Arrears a worry as African Development Bank meets.
newsitem.headline: Arrears a worry as African Development Bank meets.

text.p: The African Development Bank was warned on Wednesday that arrears on debt payments owed by African states threatened its stability, despite the profound restructuring undertaken over the past two years.
The AfDB opened its three-day annual meeting in relatively optimistic mood, but Ivory Coast's finance minister, N'Goran Niamien, warned against complacency.
Stricter lending policies meant that arrears had risen by only 5.75 percent in 1996 against 41 percent in 1995, he said.
But, he added, "these payment delays continue to represent a serious threat to our institution as regards its financial situation".
Niamien noted that the bulk of the arrears was owed by countries going through periods of political or social crisis.

But, he said, some countries felt they could drag their feet on servicing their AfDB debt while respecting payments to other multilateral organisations like the World Bank. That was not acceptable, Niamien said.
AfDB President Omar Kabbaj admitted that that "progress has been mixed" on the arrears question, but he said outstanding arrears had declined by nine percent in 1997 up to mid-April.

Total arrears currently stood at about 557 million units of account, or about $800 million, but the AfDB estimates that 80 percent of the total is owed by states with civil wars or other social problems.
However, Kabbaj, formally opening the annual meeting, said he was "reasonably optimistic" about the future of Africa.
Real gross domestic product growth in 1996 was estimated at 4.8 percent and, for the second successive year, this was higher than the population's growth rate.

The bank is looking for a capital increase, in part to devote more resources to private sector assistance, but some Western country shareholders either doubt the need for the new money or want more influence in return for handing it over.
Some African states, led by Nigeria, say African countries must retain two-thirds of the bank's shares, as at present.
Kabbaj said he hoped the board would agree to "a moderate capital increase", which he would like to see by 1999.
